title: Protein and Nutrition Basics
summary: Know the nutrients → Read the label → Compare fairly → Build a meal
subtitle: Choose everyday food with more confidence and less label confusion.

blocks.text: Some food packages print protein in letters so big that the peas inside seem to need an agent. The useful details are usually quieter, and knowing where to look makes shopping easier.
Choose food with confidence, not marketing.
blocks.detail: Knowing how much protein you need, and how to read a label, helps you build meals that fuel you, before a package makes its sales pitch.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows you how to read a label the right way.

blocks.text: Your body uses protein to build and repair tissues, including muscle. Protein is a nutrient, which means something in food your body needs. It isn’t only a product sold in a tub.
Your food choices work together over days and weeks. This regular mix is your eating pattern, and it includes vegetables, fruit, whole grains and protein foods.

Carbohydrates give you energy and are found in foods like rice, potatoes and fruit. Fibre is a type of carbohydrate in plant foods, including beans and whole grains, and it helps your bowels. Fats also give energy and help you absorb some nutrients. Foods like nuts and canola oil provide healthy unsaturated fats.
Beans, tofu, eggs and yogurt can all fit into everyday meals. Choose foods you enjoy and can get, and include plant protein foods often. A familiar meal is a good place to start.
How much protein, and where to find it

items.title: Basic daily need
items.text: About 0.8 g per kg — of body weight a day. For a 70 kg adult, that is about 56 g.

items.title: Active adults and older adults
items.text: About 1.0 to 1.6 g per kg — often helps people who strength train or are over 65 keep muscle.

items.title: Common foods
items.text: An egg has about 6 g — 3/4 cup of cooked lentils about 13 g, 3/4 cup of Greek yogurt about 15 g and 75 g of cooked chicken about 23 g.

items.title: Spread it out
items.text: Some at each meal — works better for muscle than most of it at dinner.

blocks.text: This lesson offers general food education, not a personal protein target. If you have kidney disease, a prescribed diet, food allergies or questions about your needs, ask a registered dietitian or your health care provider before changing your plan.
Start with a food you use, like a breakfast cereal or canned soup. When you compare similar products, check the amount each label describes before you compare the numbers.
The Nutrition Facts table gives protein in grams for the serving size listed. That serving is a reference amount on the label, not an instruction about how much you must eat.
Compare fairly. If two packages describe different amounts of food, compare the same amount before deciding which has more protein.
A small label calculation
Here’s a made-up label for practice: a bean mix lists 8 g of protein per 125 mL. If you eat 250 mL, that’s twice the listed serving, so you get 16 g of protein.
This math tells you what’s in that portion, not whether it meets your own needs. The example is for practising label math and isn’t a real brand.
Read the right unit. Protein in grams is an amount. A % Daily Value shown for another nutrient isn’t a protein amount or your personal protein target.
Percent Daily Value, or % DV, shows whether a serving has a little or a lot of certain nutrients. Health Canada says 5% DV or less is a little, and 15% DV or more is a lot.

Look at the whole food, not just the protein line, including sodium, fibre and saturated fat. Ingredients are listed by weight, largest first. Also check allergy information that matters to you. Packages now carry a magnifying-glass symbol on the front when they’re high in sodium, sugars or saturated fat.

items.title: “The package with the biggest protein number is always the best choice.”
items.text: The amount the label describes, the rest of the food and how it fits your meal also matter.

blocks.text: Vitamins and minerals have important jobs too. For example, vitamin D helps your body use calcium, a mineral that supports bones and teeth. No single food covers every need, which is why the mix you eat matters.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The lunch that travelled

blocks.text: The lunch that travelled
paragraphs: Farid drove a city bus in Edmonton and wanted a lunch he could enjoy during his split shift, without buying another snack at the depot. He joked that the shiny protein display at his grocery store looked ready to run for office.

One evening, a big protein claim on a soup pouch caught his eye. He bought it with some bread, expecting the pouch to be his whole lunch. Later he noticed the Nutrition Facts table described only part of the pouch.
Farid read the label again and did the math for what he would eat. He still liked the soup. But he realized a big protein number didn’t tell him whether the lunch would fill him up or fit his break.

At home, he compared another soup, using the same amount, and checked the sodium too. He had a choice: keep buying the flashy pouch, or try something new. He decided to keep the soup for now and then, and try a chickpea wrap with vegetables and fruit on his next shift.
He packed the wrap the night before and kept it cold until his break. The food worked well, but the container didn’t. It was too wide for his lunch bag and squashed the wrap against his water bottle.

Instead of buying a special meal kit, Farid used a narrower container he already owned. Over two more shifts, he adjusted how much he packed and added a snack when he wanted one. At his next grocery visit, the protein display kept its campaign promises to itself while Farid read the labels.

blocks.text: Solve the real obstacle. A good food choice still needs a container that works, a way to keep it cold and time to eat it.
Fit the food to your real day, and the habit will stick.
blocks.detail: A quick label check and a practical packing choice help you build a lunch you will eat, without buying a whole new system.
blocks.extra: Section 05 shows you how to build a simple protein bowl.

blocks.text: Choose one meal that feels awkward. Name the obstacle first, like food that’s hard to carry or a recipe that takes too long.
Adjustable example: Build a bowl
This bowl is an example, not a personal meal plan. Choose foods from what you have and compare one useful label.

items.title: Start with chickpeas, cooked brown rice and vegetables you enjoy.
Chickpeas contribute protein and fibre; rice supplies carbohydrate, and vegetables add variety.
Add a suitable dressing, such as canola oil with lemon and herbs, for flavour and unsaturated fat.
Compare similar chickpea products in equal amounts, including sodium, and plan where the meal will stay chilled.

blocks.text: Keep an easy plant option on hand. Canned beans save prep time. Low-sodium versions help, and draining and rinsing canned beans cuts sodium further.
Swap chickpeas for another protein food if you need to. Adjust the amount to suit you, and keep the meal simple if your kitchen is basic.
Frozen vegetables help when winter shopping is hard. Change one part of your routine at a time to see what helps.
Plan for food safety too. Put leftovers in the fridge within two hours, use them within 2 to 3 days or freeze them, and reheat them to 74°C, checked with a digital food thermometer.
Throw out cooked food left at room temperature for more than two hours. Smell can’t confirm it’s safe, and a cold Canadian day doesn’t turn your car into a reliable fridge.

items.title: “Learning about protein means everyone needs a protein supplement.”
items.text: Supplements aren’t automatically needed. Most people can get enough protein from food. Look at your eating pattern first, and get personal advice if you’re unsure about your needs.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Write a backup next to one shopping item, like lentils for chickpeas. It gives you a practical choice when the shelf is empty, without changing the whole meal.
Quick Check

items.title: Does a labelled serving size tell you how much you must eat?
items.text: It tells you the food amount described by the table.

items.title: An illustrative label lists 6 g of protein per portion. How much is in two equal portions?
items.text: Two equal portions provide twice the listed amount.

items.title: Can a familiar bean dish be part of a protein-food routine?
items.text: Beans are a plant protein food.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Two similar foods have different labelled serving amounts. What should you do first? A. Pick the larger number. · B. Compare equal amounts. · C. Ignore both labels.
items.text: Equal amounts make the comparison useful.

items.title: An illustrative label shows 10 g of protein per 200 mL. You eat 100 mL. How much protein is that? A. 5 g. · B. 10 g. · C. 20 g.
items.text: Half the amount in this made-up example contains half the protein: 5 g.

items.title: You want an easier lunch. Which plan fits this lesson? A. Buy a supplement before checking your meals. · B. Remove every grain food. · C. Try a suitable protein food with other foods and plan safe storage.
items.text: Consider the full meal and whether you can carry and store it safely.

items.title: Write one sentence describing a food decision you can try, including how it will fit your day.
items.text: I will compare two similar bean products and pack my chosen one with a meal in a container that fits my bag.

blocks.text: Read labels for the amount they describe, and choose protein foods within a varied eating pattern. Write one practical food decision that fits your day.

items.title: Eating pattern
items.text: What you usually eat and drink over time.

items.title: Nutrition Facts table
items.text: Label information about nutrients in a listed amount of food.

items.title: Serving size
items.text: The food amount described by a label.

items.title: Portion
items.text: The amount you choose to eat.

items.title: Percent daily value
items.text: A reference showing a little or a lot of certain nutrients in a labelled serving.
